text: Nexcess sells managed WordPress and WooCommerce hosting, so we expected this review to be simple: open the pricing page, note the plans, done. It wasn’t. When we went back to nexcess.com in 2026, the WordPress pricing page we had used before returned a “page not found” error, and the homepage now talks about bare metal, AI readiness and compliance instead of blogs and stores. The managed WordPress plans still exist. They are sold on liquidweb.com, under a logo that reads “Liquid Web by Nexcess”. So this Nexcess review covers those plans: what they cost in US dollars, what you get on Pro and Elite, the features that actually set them apart, and the gaps we could not fill. When a claim comes from the company, we say so. Quick answer Nexcess (through Liquid Web) is a good fit for a business WordPress site that wants staging, daily backups, a CDN and safer plugin updates without touching a server. Pro WordPress starts at $19 a month for one site. Elite, at $29, is the plan we’d actually buy, because it doubles the backup history and adds human migration and virtual patching. If you run a small hobby blog, you’re paying for things you won’t use. Best for Business WordPress sites that want a managed setup Entry price $19 a month billed monthly, or $17.10 a month on annual billing (one site, 50,000 visits) Plans Pro WordPress and Elite WordPress, from 1 to 25 sites and 50k to 400k monthly visits per site Backups Daily, kept 14 days on Pro and 30 days on Elite Stand-out extras Visual Comparison for plugin updates, staging, Stencils and Patchstack on Elite Not shown Renewal price and a refund period Skip it if You want the cheapest plan that works, or a published money-back promise Where Nexcess WordPress hosting lives now This part confuses people, so it’s worth a minute. Nexcess.com today is pitched at bigger infrastructure buyers. The homepage headline is about cloud, and the main menu points to managed VPS, managed dedicated servers, bare metal and a section called Sites & Stores. The Nexcess homepage now leads with cloud and bare metal, not WordPress plans (2026). Sites & Stores does list “WordPress Hosting+”, “WooCommerce Hosting+”, Magento and Shopware hosting. But there are no prices there, only a “Chat with an expert” button. If you want a plan you can buy with a card in five minutes, you end up on Liquid Web’s WordPress hosting page. How do the two fit together? Nexcess’s own site answers it. Its company description says it serves its customers “with our sub-brands LiquidWeb and Servers.com”, and it lists “Liquid Web by Nexcess” as part of the group. The Liquid Web header carries the same “by Nexcess” line under its logo, and the top bar links Nexcess.com, Servers.com and LiquidWeb.com side by side. The Liquid Web header links the three sites and its logo reads “by Nexcess” (2026). In practice, a “Nexcess WordPress plan” and a “Liquid Web WordPress plan” are the same product today. Whichever site you buy from, check that the plan names and prices match what you see below. If you also need a VPS or a dedicated server, our Liquid Web review covers the rest of the range. Nexcess prices: what you will actually pay The pricing tool asks two questions: how many sites, and how many visits each site gets per month. It then shows a Pro and an Elite card. Here is the smallest setup, one site with up to 50,000 visits, on monthly billing. Pro WordPress at $19 and Elite WordPress at $29 a month for one site, billed monthly (2026). Switch to annual billing and both drop by 10 percent. The page shows the annual price as a monthly figure and doesn’t say whether you pay the whole year up front, so confirm that at checkout. The same plans with annual billing: $17.10 and $26.10 a month (2026). For one site, this is the full price ladder we found in 2026, in US dollars: One site, monthly visits Pro monthly Pro annual (per month) Elite monthly Elite annual (per month) Up to 50,000 $19 $17.10 $29 $26.10 Up to 150,000 $39 $35.10 $59 $53.10 Up to 400,000 $79 $71.10 $119 $107.10 Each step up in visits also raises storage and bandwidth. Pro and Elite get the same resources at every size, so the price gap between them is purely about features, not horsepower. Monthly visits per site Storage Bandwidth 50k 15 GB 2 TB 150k 40 GB 3 TB 400k 100 GB 5 TB You pick two things: how many sites (1, 3, 5, 10 or 25) and how many visits each site gets. Pro and Elite share the same resources, and storage and bandwidth are shared across the sites on a plan. The jump from 50,000 to 150,000 visits roughly doubles the bill, and you get 40 GB of storage and 3 TB of bandwidth instead of 15 GB and 2 TB. Here is what that middle tier looks like on the page. One site with up to 150,000 monthly visits, billed monthly (2026). A word on “visits”. Most small business sites are nowhere near 50,000 a month. If your analytics say 8,000, don’t let the bigger tiers scare you. Start at the bottom and move up when the numbers say so. The page says you can switch to a larger plan as you grow. Hosting several sites on one plan This is where the pricing gets more interesting for freelancers and small agencies. Pick five sites and the cards show a per-site price under the total. Five sites at 50,000 visits each: $11.80 a site on Pro and $17.80 a site on Elite, billed monthly (2026). That’s a real saving over five single-site plans ($95 on Pro). The catch sits in the small print on the badges: storage and bandwidth are marked “shared”. On the five-site plan the cards still show 15 GB and 2 TB, so all five sites draw from that same pool. Five small brochure sites will fit easily. Five sites with big image libraries or WooCommerce product photos might not. The tool goes up to 10 and 25 sites. Ten sites at 50,000 visits each came to $99 a month on Pro and $169 on Elite when we checked. Some of the largest combinations showed odd numbers in our check, so price those directly on the page if you’re planning that big. Renewal, add-ons and the fine print Three things are missing from the pricing page, and each one matters for your budget. First, renewal. Shared hosts usually show a low first-term price and a much higher renewal. This page shows one price and no renewal figure at all. That could mean the price simply stays the same, which is common with managed WordPress plans billed monthly, but we could not confirm it. Look at the order summary before you pay. Second, extras. A note beside the plans says there are no hidden fees, then mentions optional add-ons such as Performance Shield and usage-based extras for autoscaling and CDN overage. Those are “listed in plan details”, which we could not see without starting an order. If your site gets sudden traffic spikes, ask how those extras are billed. Third, refunds. Neither the Liquid Web WordPress page nor the Nexcess pages we read state a money-back period. Third-party sites disagree on whether managed WordPress is covered by one. We’d rather say “we don’t know” than repeat a guess, so read the terms at checkout, or ask in chat before you buy. What every plan includes Both Pro and Elite come with the same base layer, listed in an “Included in every plan” panel: DDoS protection, a web application firewall, an edge CDN powered by Cloudflare, Object Cache Pro and Kadence Security Pro. Both plans also get automatic WordPress updates, staging sites, a self-serve migration tool and Visual Comparison. Further down, the page also promises free SSL certificates, continuous malware monitoring and regular PHP updates. One small oddity: the plan panel names Kadence Security Pro, while a section further down names the Solid Security Pro plugin as free with every plan. Either way, you get a premium security plugin without buying it. How the managed layers sit around a WordPress site (our own diagram). Why does this matter? On a cheap shared plan, you’d set up most of this yourself: a caching plugin, a Cloudflare account, a backup plugin with off-site storage, a security plugin. Here the host owns that list. Backups, staging and migrations Both plans take a backup every day. Pro keeps 14 of them and Elite keeps 30. That sounds like a small detail until you need it. Pro can roll back two weeks, Elite a full month (our own diagram). Say a plugin update quietly breaks your contact form, and nobody notices until a customer emails you three weeks later. On Pro, every backup you still have already contains the broken form. On Elite, you can go back to a copy from before the update. The same goes for malware that sits quietly for a while before anyone spots it. For a business site, those extra 16 days are the strongest reason to pay $10 more. Staging is included on both plans. You get a copy of your site where you can try a new theme, a page builder update or a checkout change before it goes live. Migration is where the plans split. Pro gives you the self-serve migration tool. Elite adds “Migration by a human”, meaning their team moves the site for you. For a simple blog, the tool is fine. For a WooCommerce store with custom code or a big database, having someone else own the move is worth a lot. Visual Comparison and Stencils These two features are what make the Nexcess platform feel different from a generic managed host. Visual Comparison handles plugin updates. According to Nexcess’s documentation, it applies a plugin update to a staging copy of your site first, takes screenshots of your priority pages, and compares them with the live site. If the pages look the same, the update goes live, either automatically or when you approve it. If something shifts past the allowed limit, the live site keeps the old version and you get a report. Update found: A plugin from wordpress.org has a new version. Staging copy: The update goes onto a copy of your site, not the live one. Screenshots: Your priority pages are captured before and after. Compare: Pages that look different past a set limit fail the check. Looks the same: The update is applied to the live site, automatically or when you approve it. Something moved: The live site keeps the old version and you see the report. The host tries the update away from your live site and compares the pages. It has limits worth knowing. The docs say it works on plugins from the wordpress.org directory, so paid plugins and themes aren’t covered, and sites over 15 GB are left out. It also only spots visual breakage. A broken payment webhook that looks fine on screen will pass. Still, for the common “plugin update wrecked my layout” problem, it’s a genuinely useful safety net, and it’s on both plans. Stencils is an Elite feature. Nexcess describes a Stencil as a saved snapshot of a site that you can use to launch new sites on the same plan, and the docs say Stencils don’t count against your disk space. If you build similar sites for clients, with the same theme, plugins and starter pages, that saves the setup routine each time. If you run one site, you’ll never touch it. Elite also adds virtual patching from Patchstack. When a security hole is found in a plugin, a virtual patch can block attacks on it before the plugin’s author releases a fix. That covers the gap between “vulnerability published” and “you updated”, which is when most WordPress sites get hit. Speed, uptime and support We didn’t load-test these plans, so this section is about what the company promises, not what we measured. On speed, the page lists multi-layered caching, the latest PHP versions, an integrated CDN and image compression. It says plans are configured to WordPress.org’s own performance requirements. On Elite, PHP workers scale up automatically during traffic spikes, which helps a store on a sale day. Object Cache Pro on both plans is a real plus for WooCommerce and membership sites, where many pages can’t be fully cached. On uptime, the claim is bold: 99.9999 percent. That’s about half a minute of downtime a year. We can’t confirm it, and the page doesn’t explain what you get if it’s missed, so treat it as a target rather than a promise with teeth. Support is described as 24/7, from people with experience across thousands of WordPress sites. The way in on the WordPress page is “Chat with an expert”. We didn’t see phone or email listed there. Nexcess’s own homepage gives phone numbers, but they appear as company contacts rather than WordPress support lines. Pro or Elite: which one to pick Honestly, for most business sites we’d take Elite. The $10 a month difference at the entry size buys 16 more days of backups, a human migration, Stencils and virtual patching. If any one of those saves you a single bad afternoon a year, it has paid for itself. Pro still makes sense if you’re careful with updates, you notice problems quickly, and you’re happy to move the site yourself. Run through these three questions: Question If yes If no 1. Do you want a human migration, Stencils or virtual patching for plugin holes? Elite WordPress. Still read questions 2 and 3. Go on to question 2. 2. Will one site pass the entry visit tier soon? Price the next visit tier before you buy. Go on to question 3. 3. Are 14 days of daily backups enough for your site? Pro WordPress covers it. Elite keeps 30 days. Three questions that settle Pro versus Elite. Who Nexcess suits Nexcess fits best when downtime or a broken update costs you money. Think of a local service business whose leads come through the website, a WooCommerce shop with steady orders, or a membership site where logged-in pages can’t be cached. The page also says managed WooCommerce uses the same plans and resources, with WooCommerce already installed. It also suits freelancers who look after a handful of client sites. The multi-site plans bring the per-site cost down, Stencils speed up new builds on Elite, and Visual Comparison takes some of the risk out of routine plugin updates across every site. Who should skip it If you run a personal blog with a few hundred visitors a month, a basic shared plan costs a fraction of this and will do the job. Our best cheap web hosting picks are a better fit. You’d be paying for staging and plugin testing you won’t use. Skip it, too, if you need lots of storage on a small budget. Fifteen GB shared across several sites fills up fast with photos and video. And if a published refund window is a must for you, this offer doesn’t show one, so you’d be buying on trust or after a chat with sales. Want to compare it with the other big managed hosts first? Our Kinsta review and WP Engine review cover two of the closest rivals, and our best WordPress hosting picks include cheaper options too. Our verdict The Nexcess WordPress plans are a solid managed option for business sites, and they’re fairly priced for what you get. Visual Comparison, 30-day backups on Elite and Patchstack virtual patching are practical features, not marketing filler. The pricing is clear on the page, and the multi-site plans are good value if your sites are small. The weak spots are about paperwork rather than hosting. The brand story is confusing right now, with WordPress plans sold on Liquid Web’s site. Renewal pricing, usage-based extras and refunds aren’t spelled out where you choose a plan. None of that is a deal-breaker, but check all three before you pay. If they check out, Elite at $29 a month is the plan we’d pick for a site that earns money. See the plans on Liquid Web Frequently asked questions How much does Nexcess WordPress hosting cost? Pro WordPress starts at $19 a month and Elite at $29 a month for one site with up to 50,000 monthly visits, billed monthly. Annual billing takes 10 percent off, which brings them to $17.10 and $26.10 a month. These are the prices we saw in 2026; renewal prices weren’t shown. Is Nexcess the same as Liquid Web? They’re part of the same group, and Nexcess describes Liquid Web as one of its sub-brands. Liquid Web’s logo reads “by Nexcess”, and today the managed WordPress plans are sold on liquidweb.com. Why can’t I find WordPress prices on nexcess.com? Because nexcess.com now sends WordPress buyers to a “Chat with an expert” button instead of a price list. The old WordPress pricing page returned a “page not found” error when we checked, and the priced plans are on Liquid Web’s WordPress hosting page. Does Nexcess include backups? Yes, every plan takes a daily backup. Pro keeps 14 days of them and Elite keeps 30 days. Can I run WooCommerce on these plans? Yes. The page says managed WooCommerce hosting uses the same plans and resources, with WooCommerce pre-installed. For a busy store, look at the 150,000 visit tier and the Elite plan’s autoscaling PHP workers. Is there a money-back guarantee? We couldn’t confirm one. Neither the Liquid Web WordPress page nor the Nexcess pages we read state a refund period, so check the terms at checkout or ask in chat before you pay. text: Our verdict Nexcess sells managed WordPress and WooCommerce hosting with a generous visit allowance for the price: $19 a month buys one site and 50,000 visits on Pro, with malware protection, Object Cache Pro, a CDN, staging and human-assisted migration included. Busy WooCommerce stores get useful extras like a sales performance monitor. The catches are real, though. The brand has been reshuffled with Liquid Web twice in a year, plan prices are hidden behind JavaScript on the official pages, the current terms say fees are non-refundable, and you must give 30 days' written notice to stop a renewal. G2 and Trustpilot scores are middling. It's a reasonable pick for a store that has outgrown cheap shared hosting, as long as you start monthly. Extra sites $9 (Pro) or $12 (Elite) a month; 100,000 extra visits $10 a month. Magento from $32.64/month with a new-customer promo. No free plan or trial Visit Nexcess What works 50,000 monthly visits on the $19 entry plan, more than Kinsta or WP Engine include at $35 Malware protection, Object Cache Pro, CDN, staging and human-assisted migration on every plan WooCommerce extras: a sales performance monitor and a plugin performance monitor First month over your visit limit is free, and overage is billed in small steps What doesn't Current terms say all fees are non-refundable; older 30-day guarantee claims are out of date Auto-renewal needs written notice at least 30 days before the term ends Confusing branding: Nexcess, Liquid Web and Servers.com share one company and overlapping sites About 3.2/5 on G2 from roughly 30 reviews, and recent Trustpilot complaints about reaching a human We have not used Nexcess. This guide to Nexcess hosting is based on Nexcess's own plan pages and terms of service (read November 13, 2026), the Liquid Web pricing page, public reviews on G2 and Trustpilot, recent independent pricing write-ups, and the plan pages of Kinsta and WP Engine. Where a figure is our own math or comes from a third party, we say so. Sources are listed at the end. The short version: Nexcess is managed WordPress, WooCommerce and Magento hosting aimed at stores and busy sites. The entry price of $19 a month buys a lot of traffic headroom. But the brand has changed shape twice in a year, and the current terms are strict: no refunds, and 30 days' written notice to stop a renewal. What Nexcess is now (and why the name is confusing) If you looked at Nexcess before, things have moved. Here's the timeline, pieced together from Nexcess's announcement and independent coverage: 2019: Liquid Web bought Nexcess, a host known for Magento and WooCommerce. Late 2025: nexcess.net began redirecting to Liquid Web, and Nexcess's own storefront closed, according to an independent deals tracker. April 8, 2026: Nexcess came back as the parent brand. Its announcement describes a "specialty cloud" that unites "the managed expertise of Liquid Web with the global bare-metal reach of Servers.com." Liquid Web is now "Liquid Web by Nexcess." Mid-2026: the old Spark, Maker and Builder plans were replaced by two plan families, Pro and Elite , according to the same tracker. The top of Liquid Web's pricing page, with links to Nexcess.com, Servers.com and LiquidWeb.com in the header, captured November 13, 2026 In practice, the managed WordPress and WooCommerce plans appear on both nexcess.com and liquidweb.com with the same specs. On nexcess.com, the "Buy now" buttons go to a Nexcess checkout. Many review sites still quote Spark and Maker prices, so check the date on anything you read. The rebrand also touched software. In May 2026, Search Engine Journal reported a backlash after Liquid Web folded its WordPress plugins (Kadence, LearnDash, The Events Calendar, Give and others) into a new lineup, with users reporting license, login and invoice problems. The company said existing customers keep their plans, pricing and license keys. A puzzled shop owner trying to work out which box their website moved into, with a cat asleep in one of them. Illustration. What Nexcess hosting includes According to the vendor, every managed WordPress and WooCommerce plan includes: Plugin and core update checks before updates go live, plus malware cleanup ("Monarx" firewall and malware protection). Object Cache Pro and an Edge CDN . A staging and a development site for each site. Human-assisted migration , free SSL and email hosting. Plugin and sales performance monitors , a live security dashboard, and 24/7/365 support. A 99.99% uptime SLA , listed on the WordPress page. Elite adds advanced malware protection (virtual patching, login and database attack protection), EdgePress on top of the CDN, 30 days of daily backups instead of 14, more PHP workers and "Stencils," site templates you can reuse when launching new sites. Nexcess's managed WooCommerce page, captured November 13, 2026 Nexcess’s website as of November 13, 2026 (screenshot). Top of the page; plan prices sit further down and were not in view Nexcess pricing in 2026: Pro and Elite plans The plan cards on Nexcess's site load their prices with JavaScript, and our tools only saw "— /month." The comparison table on the same pages shows starting prices of $19 a month for Pro and $29 a month for Elite , and the toggle says about 10% off for annual billing. Two independent sources checked in November 2026 (Gaurav Tiwari and DigitalHosting) give the same monthly figures, and Tiwari lists the yearly rate as $17.10 and $26.10 a month. Nexcess's managed WordPress page, captured November 13, 2026. Plan prices sit further down the page. Here's what each single-site tier includes. Higher tiers exist up to 12.5 million visits, but their prices weren't visible to us, so we've left them out rather than guess. Plan Price (monthly) Billed yearly Visits/month Storage Backups kept PHP workers Pro $19 about $17.10/mo ($205/yr) 50,000 20 GB 14 days 15 Elite $29 about $26.10/mo ($313/yr) 50,000 40 GB 30 days 25 Pro Not shown — 250,000 40 GB 14 days 15 Elite Not shown — 250,000 80 GB 30 days 25 Yearly totals are our own math from the per-month figures. Add-ons, from the official pages: Extra site: $9 a month on Pro, $12 on Elite. Visits and storage are shared across all sites on a plan. Visit pack: $10 a month for each extra 100,000 monthly visits. Ten-site plans start at $89 (Pro) and $119 (Elite), according to Tiwari. We couldn't see these on the official page. Nexcess says there are "no hidden fees" and no transaction fees on WooCommerce. We didn't find an intro-then-renewal price jump on the current plans. The terms do allow price increases with 30 days' notice, effective at your next renewal term. Is there a Nexcess free plan or trial? No. We found no free plan and no free trial on the current pages. See the refunds section below before you pay for a year. What happens when your site gets busy Nexcess counts visits per plan per month. You get alerts at 80% and 100% of your allowance. The first month over is free. After that, extra visits cost $0.50 per 1,000 until you add a visit pack or upgrade. Example: a WooCommerce store on Pro (50,000 visits) that grows to 120,000 visits a month. Our own math, using the official rates: Option Extra cost per month Total per month Pay overage (70,000 × $0.50 per 1,000) $35 $54 Add one visit pack (150,000 visits) $10 $29 The visit pack is the obvious fix. That's a friendlier setup than hosts that charge for overage in big blocks, but remember to add the pack before the second month. Nexcess Magento hosting Magento (Adobe Commerce) is where Nexcess built its name, and it's still sold separately. The Liquid Web pricing page lists four Magento plans with "no traffic limits," a Cloudflare-powered CDN and free autoscaling: Magento plan Storage Bandwidth Sites Starting at XS 50 GB 1 TB up to 11 $32.64/mo S 75 GB 2 TB up to 16 $64.80/mo M 125 GB 3 TB up to 21 $113.76/mo L 400 GB 5 TB up to 31 $191.52/mo These prices come with a promo ("Up to 49% off," coupons MAG49OFF and MAG52OFF) that is "valid for new accounts only." The page doesn't show the regular price, so ask what you'll pay at renewal before you sign. The Nexcess Sites & Stores page sends Magento buyers to "Chat with an expert" rather than a checkout. Refunds, cancellation and renewals This is the part to read before you pay for a year. Some review sites still promise a "30-day money-back guarantee." We couldn't find a live guarantee page, and the current Nexcess terms of service (effective October 16, 2026) say otherwise: "All Services are non-cancellable and all Fees are non-refundable" (section 3). Orders renew automatically and charge your card unless you give "written notice of its intention not to renew at least thirty (30) days before expiration of the current Term" (section 8). If you cancel early, the early termination charge is 100% of the remaining monthly fees, or 100% of a prepaid amount (section 8). Fees can go up with 30 days' notice, from the next renewal term (section 3). You're responsible for keeping your own backups of your data (section 10). Our advice: pay monthly for the first few months. If you leave, send written notice well before the 30-day cutoff and keep a copy. If a sales rep promises a refund window, get it in writing. Nexcess reviews: what users say Ratings are thin and split across brand names. G2: about 3.2/5 from roughly 30 reviews for Nexcess, according to G2's comparison pages. Positive reviews mention years without downtime and agencies running dozens of client sites; G2 also scores its free migration highly. Trustpilot (Liquid Web Inc.): 3.8/5 from 2,807 reviews, 82% 5-star and 12% 1-star, with replies to 81% of negative reviews. Nexcess's own homepage shows a 4.8 rating in its page code, which doesn't match what Trustpilot displays. The patterns in recent reviews: Praise: knowledgeable support staff, smooth complex migrations, and long-term managed WordPress customers who call it reliable. Reaching a human: several 2026 reviews say AI chat agents stood between them and human support during urgent problems. Slow tickets: some reviewers describe tickets left open for days or passed between agents. Price increases: one reviewer reports a proposed price doubling and another says prices rose after an acquisition. We didn't find a recent Reddit thread worth citing directly. Nexcess vs Kinsta and WP Engine Entry plans from each vendor's page (Kinsta figures from our best web hosting guide , checked the same day): Host Entry price Sites Visits/month Storage Refund Nexcess Pro $19/mo (about $17.10 yearly) 1 50,000 20 GB None in current terms Kinsta Single $35/mo 1 about 35,000 10 GB Full refund within 30 days WP Engine (1 site) $35/mo ($28/mo yearly) 1 25,000 10 GB Not stated on plans page Nexcess vs Kinsta: Nexcess gives more visits and storage for roughly half the price, plus email hosting and WooCommerce monitoring. Kinsta has a clear 30-day refund, a polished dashboard, and stronger review scores. If you're unsure, Kinsta is the lower-risk trial. Nexcess vs WP Engine: WP Engine's 1-site plan costs more and includes fewer visits. WP Engine has far more G2 reviews and a larger agency ecosystem. If your site is small and mostly static, managed hosting may be more than you need. Our best web hosting guide covers shared plans from about $2 a month, and our best VPS hosting guide covers self-managed servers. Is Nexcess worth it? Nexcess is worth a look when: You run a WooCommerce or Magento store where slow checkouts or malware cost real money. Your traffic is between a few thousand and a few hundred thousand visits a month, so the 50,000-visit Pro plan plus visit packs fits. You want someone else to test updates and clean up malware. It's hard to justify when: You run a simple brochure site that a $3 shared plan handles fine. You want to try a host and get your money back if it doesn't work. You won't keep track of a 30-day written notice window. Our take On paper, Nexcess is good value for managed WordPress and WooCommerce: $19 a month for 50,000 visits, malware protection, caching, staging and checkout monitoring is a better allowance than Kinsta or WP Engine offer at $35. What holds it back is everything around the product: a brand that has been reshuffled twice, prices hidden from the plan cards, a middling review record, and terms with no refunds and a 30-day renewal notice. If you run a store and want managed hosting without paying top-tier prices, start on a monthly plan, test support before you depend on it, and put your renewal date in your calendar. Managed WordPress and WooCommerce start at $19 a month for Pro and $29 for Elite, each with one site and 50,000 monthly visits. Annual billing saves about 10%. Extra sites cost $9 or $12 a month, and 100,000 extra visits cost $10 a month. Is Nexcess the same as Liquid Web? They're the same company. Since April 2026, Nexcess is the parent brand, and Liquid Web operates as "Liquid Web by Nexcess." The managed WordPress and WooCommerce plans appear on both websites with the same specs. Does Nexcess have a money-back guarantee? Not in the current terms. The terms of service effective October 16, 2026 say all fees are non-refundable. They were replaced in 2026 by Pro and Elite plans priced by monthly visits, according to independent trackers. If you're on an old plan, ask support in writing what your renewal price will be. text: Home > Hosting Reviews > Nexcess – 996 Customer Reviews: Analysis (Sep 2026) -60% Nexcess – 996 Customer Reviews: Analysis (Sep 2026) Last Update: September 3, 2026 by HowToHosting Editors 0 Comments by HowToHosting Editors | Last Update: September 3, 2026 | 0 Comments On This Page: [ hide ] Short answer: Nexcess is no longer a hosting brand you buy from. It’s the parent company name now, and the hosting is sold as Liquid Web by Nexcess. Land here looking for Nexcess WordPress plans and you’ll end up shopping on liquidweb.com. Two dates explain that. Nexcess stopped being a hosting brand of its own on 7 October 2025. That’s when nexcess.net began redirecting to liquidweb.com, and new buyers were routed to Liquid Web plans instead. On 21 April 2026, parent company CloudOne Digital relaunched Nexcess as its global brand and renamed the hosting arm “Liquid Web by Nexcess.” The name that had just been retired became the name on top. Any review describing Nexcess as a standalone host with its own price list describes a company that no longer operates that way. This review draws on 2,778 aggregated customer reviews, live checkout pricing pulled in September 2026, the published terms, and Reddit threads. Unlike affiliate-heavy reviews, we quote what the binding contract actually says about refunds. We also separate reviews the company asked for from reviews people wrote unprompted. Those two groups tell very different stories. Overall assessment: Nexcess scores 3.8/5 across 2,778 reviews. Strengths are flat WordPress pricing with no renewal jump, real 24/7 phone support, and strong hardware. The most common complaints involve slow ticket response since a 2026 support restructure, and a contract that says fees are non-refundable. Best suited for agencies and stores that need managed WordPress or WooCommerce and can pay monthly. Last updated: September 2026. Pricing and review data verified. Visit Site Nexcess Summary Name Nexcess Total Reviews 996 Average Score 4.5 Website http://nexcess.net Address 21700 Melrose Avenue Southfield , MI 48075 US Server Locations United States, Netherlands, United Kingdom, Australia Visit Nexcess Number of Reviews 996 A lot * With Nexcess recognized as the focus of this article, know that the data hereby included is taken from over 996 reviews. That should be a good observation into the quality of this hosting. Avg. Review Score 4.5 Positive * Scoring 4.5 on average is a confirmation on how great the workforce behind Nexcess are. Customer Support Positive Rating * Tech Support teams working for Nexcess are praised by people, for the most part. That suggests competence and huge rate of effectiveness. Features and Services Nexcess sells managed hosting through three brands, priced and supported differently. Hosting Types Offered Managed WordPress – the core product, priced by site count and monthly visitors Managed WooCommerce – same tier structure, tuned for stores Managed Magento – for larger catalogues VPS, managed or self-managed – a VPS (virtual private server) is a slice of a physical machine reserved for you alone Dedicated servers, managed or self-managed – a whole physical machine Cloud Dedicated and Cloud Sites – multi-site environments for agencies Bare metal through the Servers.com by Nexcess brand There’s no cheap shared hosting here. Entry is USD 9/mo for one WordPress site, which puts Nexcess above the budget hosts and below the premium managed crowd. Key Features Customers Highlight Support that answers the phone – 24/7 phone lines for the Americas, Australia and the UK, which most managed WordPress rivals don’t offer Object Cache Pro and Performance Shield – included on every WordPress plan rather than sold as add-ons Staging sites on all tiers – a staging site is a private copy where you test changes before they go live Human migration – included from the Pro tier up; Essentials gives you a self-service tool instead Backups with real retention tiers – 7, 14 or 30 days of daily backups depending on plan Data Center Locations Here’s where transparency starts to wobble. Nexcess.com says “16 global data centers.” Liquid Web’s own About page says “22 state-of-the-art data centers.” Same company, same year, two numbers. We could confirm a Michigan cluster, the company’s home state, plus a Phoenix, Arizona facility run by PhoenixNAP rather than Nexcess. Location drives latency, the delay between a visitor’s browser and your server. US visitors will see good numbers. Everyone else should ask sales which building their plan lands in. Performance Expectations We found no independent benchmark data for the current Nexcess platform. What we did find is a stack of contradictory uptime promises across the company’s own pages. The managed WordPress page advertises a “99.9999% power and network SLA.” An SLA is a Service Level Agreement, a contractual uptime promise with a penalty attached. The VPS page promises “a 99.9% server uptime guarantee.” Dedicated and WooCommerce both say 99.99%. The published SLA document promises 100% network uptime, with credit worth 10 times the downtime. Four numbers. The gap isn’t cosmetic: 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month, 99.9999% allows under three seconds. Only the SLA document binds anyone, and part of it was last updated in 2013. Customer Experience Across 2,778 reviews the score is 3.8/5. The distribution is the interesting part: 82.4% are 5-star and 11.2% are 1-star, with almost nothing between. A simple average of that spread lands near 4.4, so why is the score 3.8? Because only 187 of those 2,778 reviews were written in the last 12 months, and recent sentiment runs worse. Older reviews quoting 4.5 or higher aren’t lying. They’re describing a different period. Who Wrote the Review Changes the Score Trustpilot labels whether a review came from a company invitation or was posted unprompted. We tallied the 160 most recent. The split is stark. Of 86 invited reviews, 83 were 5-star. They average 4.9. Of 74 unprompted reviews, 52 were 1-star. They average 2.0. That’s a gap of nearly three points on a five-point scale, from the same company in the same months. Neither set is fake. Invited reviews mostly follow a solved ticket, so they catch Nexcess on a good day. Unprompted ones get written when someone is angry enough to seek out Trustpilot unasked. The first group shows you routine support. The second shows you what happens when something goes badly wrong. What Customers Praise Individual support engineers get named and thanked constantly. Reviewers credit specific people for staying on chat for hours to bring sites back after security incidents. It’s the strongest theme in the positive reviews. Response speed comes second. Multiple reviewers describe getting a knowledgeable human quickly and having the root cause explained, not just patched. Nexcess also answers criticism: it replies to 94% of its negative reviews, typically within 48 hours. Long-tenure customers on the Michigan data centers report stability. One agency running several dozen stores for five to six years called the Michigan facilities “not bad compared to others.” Common Complaints Ticket response time dominates the negative reviews. Complaints describe multi-day waits and canned answers that miss the question. One reviewer with four cPanel servers over seven years wrote that support “used to be great. Now, it is horrible.” Billing errors come second. Customers report being charged after receiving a cancellation confirmation email. That connects to a contract term most buyers never read, covered below. Third is the Phoenix outage. A cooling failure at the PhoenixNAP facility took Cloud Sites offline for more than 24 hours on 13 and 14 August 2026. In fairness, that building hosts multiple providers, and commenters reported Namecheap going down in the same incident. Nexcess didn’t own the failure, but customers still absorbed it. Community Feedback (Reddit & Forums) Community discussions run harsher than the review platforms, and cluster on one theme: a 2026 support restructure. The highest-engagement thread is “Avoid Liquid Web plugins” in r/Wordpress from June 2026, with 166 upvotes and 110 comments. Its author waited two weeks for a reply about a licence that wouldn’t validate. Commenters identifying themselves as former support staff described dedicated per-product teams being dissolved. We can’t verify anyone’s employment, so treat those as claims. The volume is verifiable though: seven separate r/Wordpress threads between May and August 2026 describe the same licensing and support problems. The churn theme is just as consistent. r/webhosting carries a steady run of departure threads: “I Left Liquid Web After 10 Years,” “15+ years with LiquidWeb, time to move on?” and “When did Liquid Web lose its way?” Several name KnownHost as where they went. The author of that last thread wrote that the company “was literally a lifesaver,” and that now they “take multiple days to solve basic issues.” One caution if you research this yourself. The r/NexcessOfficial subreddit posts near-daily and reads like community discussion. It’s the company’s own marketing channel, not customer feedback. Support Quality Support runs 24/7 across phone, live chat and tickets, with numbers for the Americas, Australia and the UK. Real phone support at USD 9/mo is unusual in managed WordPress. The catch is consistency. In our sample of the 160 most recent reviews, chat and phone contacts draw warm praise while ticket-based ones produce the 1-star reviews. Solvable on a call? The experience is good. Needs a ticket? Expect to wait. When to Use Nexcess Nexcess is a strong choice in specific cases: Ideal For Agencies running client WordPress or WooCommerce sites: Multi-site tiers, staging on every plan and human migration from Pro up are built for this work. Just size the storage tier, not the site count. Stores that need someone to answer the phone: When a checkout breaks, a phone number beats a ticket queue. Few managed WordPress hosts at this price offer one. Buyers who hate renewal surprises: On WordPress and WooCommerce, the advertised price is the recurring price. No three-year lock-in, no quiet tripling. You’ll Appreciate It If You want monthly billing without a penalty, because Nexcess prices monthly by default You need Magento hosting, which few managed hosts still support properly Your audience is American, because the Michigan facilities have the longest track record You need HIPAA-adjacent arrangements, because customers report the company signs Business Associate Agreements When NOT to Use Nexcess No host suits everyone. Nexcess isn’t right for you if: Look Elsewhere If You need a refund safety net: The Terms of Service, effective 8 May 2024, say “all Services are non-cancellable and all Fees are non-refundable.” The only money-back guarantee left in the published policies sits in a tariff document effective 17 March 2016. It’s scoped to “shared hosting only,” a product line the company no longer sells that way. Buy monthly, so a mistake costs you one month. You’re hosting many small sites cheaply: The storage ceiling makes multi-site plans poor value below the top visitor tier. Twenty-five sites sharing 15 GB is not a real offer for most agencies. You want current-generation dedicated hardware: The entry dedicated lineup runs 2018 to 2020 Intel Xeons. Bare metal specialists will give you newer silicon for the money. Hosting is sold as Liquid Web by Nexcess at liquidweb.com. Nexcess.net redirects there. Existing customers still log in at my.nexcess.net, and support emails still use @nexcess.net addresses. Is Nexcess good for beginners? Yes, with one caveat. The entry WordPress plan is USD 9/mo, includes staging and automatic updates, and comes with 24/7 phone support. Is Nexcess worth the price? On managed WordPress, yes. USD 9/mo with no renewal increase is fair, and most rivals raise the price after year one. On VPS and dedicated, be careful. The 50% discount lasts only two months, so a USD 36/mo VPS costs USD 72/mo from month three. Judge those plans at the full rate. What do customers complain about most? Three things. Slow ticket responses, which grew louder after a 2026 support restructure. Billing errors, including charges after a cancellation was confirmed. And the August 2026 Phoenix outage, which took Cloud Sites down for over 24 hours. Note that phone and chat get consistently better reviews than tickets. Does Nexcess offer refunds? Not under the current contract. The Terms of Service effective 8 May 2024 say “all Services are non-cancellable and all Fees are non-refundable.” Older reviews citing a 30-day money-back guarantee are quoting a 2016 tariff document that covers shared hosting only. Also plan ahead: cancelling requires written notice 30 days before your term ends. How does Nexcess compare to other managed WordPress hosts? It’s mid-priced and support-heavy rather than feature-heavy. Nexcess beats most rivals on phone access and on flat renewal pricing. It loses on multi-site value, because storage is tied to your visitor tier and not your site count. Twenty-five sites on the cheapest tier share just 15 GB. title: Liquid Web Review 2026: Is It Still Good Hosting for WordPress?
headings: Who owns Liquid Web now? The 2026 Nexcess changes
What we measured from the outside
text: Liquid Web is worth considering when your business needs a managed server and a team to help run it. Its cheaper WordPress plans broaden the appeal, but check the support and refund terms carefully. A small site is likely to find a simpler fit with a budget host. The earlier pricing image includes an Essentials offer. The current public page emphasizes Pro and Elite, as explained below. Who owns Liquid Web now? The 2026 Nexcess changes Liquid Web now presents itself within the Nexcess group. Its server products, managed WordPress plans and WordPress software are separate offers, even when they share a parent company. The current managed WordPress page links to Liquid Web’s sites portal. Do not assume an older Nexcess checkout, support package or refund offer applies to every present product. The order form and management level are more important to the purchase than the brand history. Plans and pricing Liquid Web still sells no shared hosting. All prices below are in US dollars, before tax, as of October 2026. Managed WordPress and WooCommerce The current public page presents Pro at $19 monthly and Elite at $29 for one site with 50,000 monthly visits, 15 GB shared storage and 2 TB bandwidth. Annual billing advertises a 10% saving. Higher traffic and multi-site combinations need their own quote or checkout check. The earlier review and screenshot included a $9 Essentials offer. That tier is not displayed in the refreshed public plan section, so do not budget a new account from that old entry price without confirmation. Pro lists daily backups retained for 14 days, staging and visual update comparison. Elite extends retention to 30 days and advertises additional assistance and store-management tools. Self-service migration is available, while the page specifically promotes human-assisted migration on Elite. The listed common features include a firewall, DDoS protection, Cloudflare-powered CDN, Object Cache Pro and Kadence Security Pro. Performance Shield is now described as an optional add-on, so it should not be treated as included in every price. The current page leaves some larger configuration prices blank. Confirm the full cart amount, resource allowance and optional usage charges before comparing a large plan with the base one-site offer. The vendor’s feature image uses an uptime figure that needs to be read alongside the applicable written SLA. VPS hosting An earlier half-price VPS promotion. The current written prices use the regular rates, rather than assuming that opening offer still applies. This is where Liquid Web is strongest. A VPS comes self-managed (you run the server) or fully managed (Liquid Web runs it), with Linux or Windows and a choice of cPanel, Plesk, or InterWorx. Fully managed VPS: The current managed-VPS page lists $72 monthly for the 4 GB entry server, followed by $100, $145 and $178 options with more resources. The earlier screenshot shows a half-price opening promotion, which is not the regular rate now displayed. Confirm the selected configuration and any control-panel or backup extras before ordering. The distinction between self-managed and fully managed matters more than the lowest VPS price. A cheaper self-managed server leaves operating-system and application work with you. Choose it only if you have the people and time to perform that work. Dedicated servers Dedicated hardware is a separate product with different resource, backup and management choices. Request a current configuration rather than applying the WordPress plan’s support or refund assumptions to a server contract. Contract and refund terms Read this before you buy. Liquid Web’s terms of service (effective May 8, 2024) say that, except where stated otherwise, “all Fees are non-refundable.” None of the pricing pages advertised a money-back guarantee as of October 2026. The terms reviewed here also say: Plans renew automatically unless you give 30 days’ written notice before the term ends. Cancelling before the end of a term means paying the rest of it: 100% of the remaining monthly charges, or 100% of a prepaid amount. Liquid Web can raise fees with 30 days’ notice, taking effect at your next renewal. Start on monthly billing if you are unsure, and note the 30-day notice deadline if you sign up for longer. WordPress plans check out through Nexcess, so ask sales which terms apply before you buy. Features that matter Management levels determine what support will actually handle. Hardware and network coverage is different from operating-system work, PHP troubleshooting or help with a control panel. Confirm that scope in the plan, not just the word managed in a headline. The vendor’s management tiers cover different kinds of work. They are separate from the WordPress plan names. For WordPress, backup retention and staging are practical differences between plans. Keep an independent backup too; our backup plugin roundup covers options. A staging plugin may help on a plan without staging, but it does not reproduce the hosting provider’s full managed-update service. Speed and uptime What the SLA really promises The top of Liquid Web’s SLA page. Liquid Web’s SLA page says it “guarantees network uptime to be 100%” for all services. The fine print matters: What counts: “all major routing devices within our network are reachable.” It covers the network, not your website. What does not count: scheduled maintenance, hardware and software maintenance, attacks such as DDoS, legal actions, and cPanel update problems. The credit: 10 times the downtime. One hour down earns 10 hours of credit. The remedy paragraph names dedicated hosting clients as eligible. The cap: credits can never exceed your monthly fee, and you must ask within 5 business days of the incident. Hardware: on dedicated servers, failed hardware is replaced “in most cases” within 30 minutes, again with a 10 times credit. A separate Nexcess SLA on the same page promises 100% network transit and power, with 5% credits per 15 minutes of outage. Product pages quote different numbers: 99.99% on the VPS and WooCommerce pages, 99.9% on the managed VPS page, and 99.9999% on the managed WordPress page. Treat the SLA page as the written promise, and ask sales which section covers your plan. What we measured from the outside We have not benchmarked a WordPress site in our own Liquid Web account. The earlier results below are public-page snapshots, not an uptime test or a controlled comparison of hosting plans. Liquid Web’s public homepage responded in a median 0.18 seconds and scored 45 mobile and 96 desktop in Lighthouse. The customer-story example stober.com responded in 0.40 seconds and scored 51/74. Different public sites do not show how the same WordPress installation would perform on different hosting plans. liquidweb.com is served through Cloudflare, so its quick response mostly reflects Cloudflare, not a Liquid Web server. Stober is named in Liquid Web’s customer stories, and its domain pointed to Liquid Web’s own network that day. Its first byte took about 0.4 seconds including connection setup. Lighthouse timed the server’s own response at about 0.13 seconds, which is quick; the low mobile score comes from the page’s images and scripts. These are snapshots from one place on one day. They say nothing about uptime, support, or how your own site would perform. Support Support is the reason most people pick Liquid Web, and it runs 24/7/365. The support page lists live chat and support cases (tickets); the VPS FAQ also mentions phone support. The big change is the response-time promise. In 2020, Liquid Web guaranteed a reply within 59 seconds on phone and chat and 59 minutes on tickets, with credits if it missed. The current SLA page says something different: The “Response Time” section of Liquid Web’s SLA page. The team “strives” to answer chats in under one minute and tickets within one hour, but these “are not part of an SLA and are not guaranteed.” Fast support is still the aim, with no written promise behind it. How much help you get also depends on your plan: on self-managed servers, support covers hardware and network only. We have not opened a current support case. A published response target and an uptime credit do not establish how quickly a WordPress problem will actually be resolved.
